Learning to Generate in the Right Order

Julius Erbach†\dagger,‡\ddagger  Dominik Narnhofer†\dagger  Bernt Schiele‡\ddagger
Jan Eric Lenssen‡\ddagger,¶  Konrad Schindler†\dagger
†\daggerETH Zurich ¶Saarland University ‡\ddaggerMax Planck Institute for Informatics, Saarland Informatics Campus
Abstract

We introduce PONDER, a method that learns in which order an image generator should fill in content and which of its earlier predictions to revise. Masked generative models construct a sample by repeatedly filling in subsets of missing variables. The order of these partial predictions determines the context available in subsequent steps and therefore affects the quality of the final sample. Common strategies are to choose the order randomly or based on local confidence estimates. Conditioned on the partially generated sample and the generator’s features, our policy chooses which positions to fill next and/or which previously filled positions to mask for later regeneration, a mechanism we call rethinking. In this way, the generation process is able to adapt to the evolving context and also to revise earlier predictions. We optimize the policy using group-relative policy gradients, with rewards that measure constraint satisfaction, human preference, or distribution quality. For the latter, we introduce FIDgrad, an image-level reward derived from the (first-order) change in Fréchet Inception Distance caused by adding a generated sample to the current feature distribution. With the generators frozen, learned ordering reduces MAR-B ImageNet FID from 4.09 to 2.78 and raises the accuracy on hard visual Sudokus from 3.9% to 56.6%, surpassing uncertainty-based greedy ordering (38.7%). Rethinking further improves these results to 2.70 FID and 96.7% accuracy, while increasing the rethinking budget of a fixed policy yields continued improvements at inference time. Our code is available here.

1 Introduction

Standard diffusion models generate images by iteratively denoising all spatial locations jointly (Ho et al., 2020; Lipman et al., 2023; Karras et al., 2022; Rombach et al., 2022). An alternative is to factorize generation over spatial locations, using a diffusion model to predict individual patches or subsets conditioned on content that has already been generated (Li et al., 2024). In this setting, the generation order becomes consequential because each prediction determines the context available for subsequent ones. It has been shown that such conditional generation is capable of high-quality image synthesis and spatial reasoning (Fan et al., 2025; Wewer et al., 2025), but also that its performance depends substantially on the chosen patch ordering (Fan et al., 2025; Wewer et al., 2025).

If all conditionals were known exactly, different orderings would yield equivalent factorizations. However, the conditionals that are actually learned do not preserve the equivalence. In practice, generation order substantially affects sample quality (Wewer et al., 2025; Li et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2025). This observation leads to a natural question: Can we learn to adapt the ordering in a sample-dependent way, such that the complete, final sample has the best possible quality?

There are three common strategies to define the order: Fixed schedules, most often in raster-scan order, are independent of the generated content (Esser et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2026; Z.ai, 2026). Random schedules sample a permutation per roll-out, as in masked autoregressive models (Li et al., 2024). These decorrelate training from any particular order but provide no mechanism for exploiting context during inference. Greedy schedules prioritize positions according to confidence or (predicted) difficulty: MaskGIT (Chang et al., 2022; Li et al., 2026) unmasks the tokens the generator is most confident about, SRM (Wewer et al., 2025) selects the ones with the lowest predicted uncertainty, and Patch Forcing (Schusterbauer et al., 2026) estimates a per-patch difficulty score and advances easy regions first, so as to obtain more context for harder ones. All three families share the same limitation: either the order of generation is completely independent of the sample being generated, or it is determined by a greedy one-step proxy.

Among those strategies, only greedy confidence-based schedules adapt the ordering to the intermediate, partial state at all. However, the decision is based on an extremely local proxy: it prioritizes positions that are easy to predict given the current context. Such a strategy does not consider how complex future steps will become based on that decision. Thus, a local prediction that is made with high confidence does not, by itself, mean that it will greatly improve the global sample quality. A highly predictable position may provide little useful context, whereas a less certain one may establish useful structure that constrains further patches.

The delayed effect of intermediate decisions turns generative modeling into a sequential decision-making problem, driven by a policy that selects positions conditioned on the current partial sample. Taking that view further, earlier predictions made with limited context may become inconsistent at later stages of the generation process, calling for a mechanism to also revisit earlier choices.

We introduce Ponder (Policy for Ordering, Next-element DEcisions and Rethinking), a scheme for learning a policy that controls the sequence order during generation, including removal of earlier predictions for subsequent regeneration. To that end, we make the following contributions:

  • •

    Learned ordering for continuous generators. A policy trained with final-sample rewards that decides where a frozen generator fills content next. It requires only the policy’s own action probabilities, not the generator’s likelihoods, which makes it the first such approach applicable to continuous-token generators with diffusion heads.

  • •

    A rethinking strategy, where the policy learns which earlier predictions to discard and regenerate as new context becomes available. This enables adaptive revision during sequential generation with a controllable rethinking budget that can be varied at inference time.

  • •

    FIDgrad, a reward function that turns a distribution-level objective into an image-level reinforcement learning signal. By estimating each sample’s first-order effect on Fréchet Inception Distance, FIDgrad enables a generation policy that directly targets quality at the distribution level.

A suite of experiments demonstrates the generality of Ponder across class-conditional generation, text-to-image synthesis, and visual constraint solving. With learned ordering alone, it reduces MAR-B ImageNet FID from 4.09 to 2.78, improves MaskGen-KL-XL HPSv2 from 24.50 to 26.50, and raises hard-Sudoku accuracy from 3.9% to 56.6%. Rethinking further improves these results, to 2.70 FID, 27.80 HPSv2 at R=32R=32, and 96.7% accuracy. Moreover, performance continues to improve as the inference-time budget increases while the policy and generator remain fixed (Figure 1).

2 Related Work

Masked generation with continuous representations.

Masked generative models predict missing content from a partially observed sample, allowing generation to proceed in different orders autoregressively. MaskGIT (Chang et al., 2022) uses discrete image tokens and iterative confidence-based decoding. MAR (Li et al., 2024) instead models conditional distributions over continuous patches using a patch-wise diffusion head, removing the need for vector quantization. FLUID (Fan et al., 2025) studies the effects of token representation and generation order in text-to-image synthesis, finding advantages for continuous tokens and random-order generation. MaskGen (Kim et al., 2025) supports both discrete and continuous representations through compact one-dimensional image tokens. We build on continuous masked generators and learn how to use their conditional predictions while keeping their weights frozen.

Adaptive and learned generation orders.

SRM (Wewer et al., 2025) demonstrates the importance of sequentialization and generation order for reasoning over continuous spatial variables, using predicted uncertainty to select the next position. Patch Forcing (Schusterbauer et al., 2026) learns per-patch difficulty estimates and adapts denoising progress across an image, allowing easier regions to provide context for harder ones. These approaches motivate adapting generation to the current sample. Our policy is trained against rewards on the completed image. Learned ordering has also been studied in discrete diffusion language models. DCoLT (Huang et al., 2025) uses final-answer rewards to optimize the reverse generation trajectory and its LLaDA generator jointly trains a token-unmasking model and the language model, adapting both generation order and token predictions. Hong et al. (2026) isolate the ordering component by keeping the language model frozen and learning a position-selection policy from verifiable terminal rewards, with regularization relative to confidence-based reference policies. Fox et al. (2026) approach ordering through variational inference: a posterior conditioned on complete training examples provides a learning signal for an inference-time token selector through an evidence lower bound. Concurrent work by Ouyang et al. (2026) learns an unmasking controller with group-relative policy optimization for multimodal diffusion language models. All of these methods operate on discrete tokens and only decide which masked position to reveal next; once revealed, a token stays fixed. Several also rely on quantities that continuous generators with a diffusion head do not provide, such as token confidences or likelihoods. Our work studies continuous-latent diffusion generators and additionally learns which previously generated positions to remove and later regenerate under a rethinking budget.

Revision during generation.

Allowing accepted predictions to change can correct errors that become apparent as additional context is generated. Path Planning (Peng et al., 2025) augments masked discrete diffusion sampling with planners that can select both masked and previously unmasked tokens for updating. It also derives an evidence lower bound for training planners with a frozen denoiser. Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion-Image (Li et al., 2026) enables revision of discrete image tokens through an augmented corruption objective and confidence-thresholded token replacement at inference. Ponder learns revision decisions from final-sample rewards without retraining the generator. Its position-selection policy allocates a prescribed removal budget: removed content is excluded from subsequent context and regenerated when its position is selected again. This separates the decision to discard a prediction from its later regeneration.

Reward optimization for generative models.

DDPO (Black et al., 2024) formulates diffusion denoising as a sequential decision process and optimizes generator parameters using downstream rewards. Flow-GRPO (Liu et al., 2025) extends group-relative policy optimization to flow matching models, while Mask-GRPO (Luo et al., 2025) develops reward-based post-training for masked text-to-image generators. Ponder applies reinforcement learning to the position-selection policy, leaving content generation to the frozen model. The optimized action probabilities are those of selecting positions to fill or remove, so policy training does not require evaluating the likelihood of generated continuous content.

Distributional objectives.

FD-loss (Yang et al., 2026) optimizes representation-space Fréchet distance by maintaining a large feature population through a queue or moving moments while backpropagating through the current generated batch. FIDgrad shares the use of evolving population statistics but derives a scalar reward reflecting the incfluence of a single sample on the FID. It measures the first-order effect of adding probability mass at a generated image’s feature. This reward trains the position-selection policy through policy gradients, without differentiating through the generator or feature extractor. It therefore connects a distributional quality objective to discrete generation and revision decisions over continuous content.

3 Method

Sequential image generation can be cast as masked image modeling. Starting from an empty canvas, the generator unmasks one or multiple regions (in practice: patches) and fills them by generating suitable pixel values or latents. That process is repeated in autoregressive fashion until the entire canvas has been filled. The goal of Ponder is to devise a policy in which order to unmask the patches. Additionally, the policy can also choose to re-mask patches, such that they can be regenerated in subsequent steps. The policy is trained to maximize a suitable target metric for the task at hand, e.g., FID (Heusel et al., 2017a) or Human Preference Score (Wu et al., 2023b).

3.1 Policy-Guided Masked Generation

Image generation proceeds for LL iterations indexed by t=0,…,L−1t=0,\ldots,L-1. Each iteration consists of three steps: evaluating the generator backbone for the current canvas x(t)x^{(t)}, selecting patches to unmask, and updating the canvas by generating content for the unmasked patches. At each iteration, the input to the backbone are image tokens for the patches that are already visible and MASK tokens for the patches that are still masked. The backbone is evaluated once and computes per-patch features that remain fixed throughout the iteration and constitute the input h(t)h^{(t)} for the policy. For diffusion-based approaches, the backbone features are concatenated with the initial noise. Note that the iterations of the sequential generator are different from the ”inner loop” of denoising steps during diffusion.

The goal of the generation process is to fill all writeable patches 𝒲⊆{1,…,N}\mathcal{W}\subseteq{\{1,\ldots,N}\}. A prescribed schedule determines the number KtK_{t} of patches to be unmasked in each iteration, while the policy chooses their locations StS_{t}. A binary visibility mask m(t)∈{0,1}Nm^{(t)}\in\{0,1\}^{N} indicates which positions are already visible as context. Optionally, there may be additional class or text conditioning cc. Using the context computed at the start of the iteration, the generator fills the selected patches and the mask is updated to the new state:

xSt(t+1)=gϕ​(x(t),St,ϵSt(t),m(t),c),mSt(t+1)=¬mSt(t)\begin{split}x^{(t+1)}_{S_{t}}&=g_{\phi}\!\big(x^{(t)},S_{t},\epsilon^{(t)}_{S_{t}},m^{(t)},c\big),\\ m^{(t+1)}_{S_{t}}&=\neg m^{(t)}_{S_{t}}\,\end{split} (1)

where gϕg_{\phi} denotes the generator and ϵSt(t)\epsilon^{(t)}_{S_{t}} is the noise initialization at the selected positions. Moreover, we extend the policy with a rethinking mode. Formally, the selection StS_{t} may contain already visible patches (mi(t)=1m_{i}^{(t)}=1), which are then reverted back to the masked state (mi(t+1)=0m_{i}^{(t+1)}=0).

3.2 Adaptive Patch Selection

The policy πθ\pi_{\theta} is a bidirectional transformer that maps the generator features h(t)h^{(t)} and start noise vectors to output logits. The policy obtains the same information that the patch-wise diffusion heads obtain. We ablate this choice in Table 5. The output logits consist of KtK_{t} sets of per-patch logits, one for each decision to be taken in the current iteration (Fig. 2). Patches are sampled sequentially, excluding those that have already been selected in the same iteration.

Let 𝒞t,k\mathcal{C}_{t,k} denote the candidate patches for decision kk. The probability of the ordered selections is

πθ(at,1:Kt∣h(t))=∏k=1Ktπθ,k(at,k∣h(t),𝒞t,k).\pi_{\theta}(a_{t,1:K_{t}}\mid h^{(t)})=\prod_{k=1}^{K_{t}}\pi_{\theta,k}(a_{t,k}\mid h^{(t)},\mathcal{C}_{t,k}). (2)

All decisions within an iteration share the same generator features. Earlier selections affect later ones only through the candidate mask. After selection, the generator fills St={at,1,…,at,Kt}S_{t}=\{a_{t,1},\ldots,a_{t,K_{t}}\} using the same context from the previous iteration for all of them. Without rethinking, the complete sequence to a complete output visits every writable patch exactly once.

3.3 Pondering by Revisiting Patches

Restricting the generation order to strict permutations simplifies the process, but makes it impossible to correct early decisions after additional context becomes available. To enable such revisions, we allow the policy to remove previously generated content. We note that the same patch selection policy can control both generation and revision. Only a minor change is needed, namely to allow the selection of already visible patches. Whenever a masked patch is selected in iteration tt, it is filled. When an unmasked patch is selected, it is returned to the masked state, thus excluding it from the backbone evaluation in the next iteration t+1t+1. The patch then remains masked until the policy selects it again, at which point it is regenerated using the new context.

Because backbone features are computed before position selection, removal does not change the features used within the current round and requires no additional backbone evaluation in that round. The next scheduled backbone evaluation uses the updated mask.

We prescribe a rethinking budget of RR removal actions. Starting from a fully masked canvas, completing the sample requires NN net fill actions. Each removal cancels one previous fill and therefore requires one additional fill later in the roll-out. A trajectory with RR removals consequently contains N+RN+R fill actions and RR removal actions, for a total of

T=N+2​RT=N+2R (3)

patch decisions. A patch may be removed more than once, with each removal counting toward the budget. Book-keeping of legal decisions ensures completion: removals are disabled once the budget is exhausted and in the final iteration L−1L-1. Conversely, they are forced when necessary to exhaust the budget before the final iteration.

Importantly, rethinking is distinct from repeatedly resampling a position under the same context, because regeneration can happen after other parts of the canvas have been filled, providing more context for the generator. The policy therefore learns not only where to generate next, but also when an earlier prediction is worth revisiting. This differs from fixed refinement schedules that allocate additional computation independently of the evolving sample.

Setting R=0R=0 recovers adaptive ordering without rethinking. Because RR changes the roll-out horizon but not the frozen generator or the policy parameterization, it can be varied at inference time within the schedules supported by the policy.

3.4 Group-Relative Policy Optimization

We train the ordering policy from a terminal reward ℛ⁡(x(L),c)\mathcal{R}(x^{(L)},c) evaluated on the completed sample. For each input and conditioning value, we generate a group of GG trajectories. Members of a group share the same initial canvas and generator noise, but sample their policy actions independently, to isolate the effect of the generation order on the final image and the associated reward. Let rjr_{j} denote the terminal reward of trajectory jj, and let r¯\bar{r} and ss denote the group mean and population standard deviation. We assign every decision in trajectory jj the advantage

Aj={(rj−r¯)/s,s>10−5,0,otherwise.A_{j}=\begin{cases}(r_{j}-\bar{r})/s,&s>10^{-5},\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (4)

Index the T=N+2​RT=N+2R primitive position decisions by dd. Let oj​do_{jd} contain the policy observation and legal candidate set at decision dd of trajectory jj. At optimizer update uu, we minimize

ℒu(θ)=−1G​T∑j=1G∑d=1T[sg(Aj)logπθ(aj​d∣oj​d)],\mathcal{L}_{u}(\theta)=-\frac{1}{GT}\sum_{j=1}^{G}\sum_{d=1}^{T}\left[\operatorname{sg}(A_{j})\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{jd}\mid o_{jd})\right], (5)

Here sg\operatorname{sg} stops gradients. We average this loss across independently collected groups.

Gradients update only the ordering policy, whereas the generator remains frozen. Batching several independent groups averages the loss across groups. We use a single policy-gradient update per collected roll-out batch, without reference-policy penalty, importance ratios, clipping, or repeated optimization over the same roll-out. Further training details are given in Appendix A.1.

3.5 Distribution-Level Optimization with FIDgrad

Standard rewards, like constraint satisfaction or human preference, can be evaluated independently for each generated sample. In contrast, population-level quality metrics, like the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID), measure the discrepancy between the distributions of generated and real images and cannot directly be broken down into per-sample rewards. Inspired by the FD-loss (Yang et al., 2026) for generative model training, we introduce FIDgrad: a reward that scores each generated image by its first-order effect on the FID of the current generative distribution. This makes it possible to optimize distribution quality through reinforcement learning, while keeping the generative model frozen.

Let qq denote the distribution of Inception features z=f⁡(x)z=f(x) of the generated images, with mean μg\mu_{g} and covariance Σg\Sigma_{g}. And let μr,Σr\mu_{r},\Sigma_{r} be the corresponding statistics of the real image data. We work with the standard Gaussian plug-in functional, which depends on qq only through its first two moments,

FID⁡(q,preal)=‖μg−μr‖22+tr⁡(Σg)+tr⁡(Σr)−2​tr​[(Σr1/2​Σg​Σr1/2)1/2].\operatorname{FID}(q,p_{\mathrm{real}})=\|\mu_{g}-\mu_{r}\|_{2}^{2}+\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_{g})+\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_{r})-2\operatorname{tr}\!\left[\big(\Sigma_{r}^{1/2}\Sigma_{g}\Sigma_{r}^{1/2}\big)^{1/2}\right]. (6)

To turn Eq. 6 into a per-sample quantity, we ask how it responds to placing a small amount of probability mass at a single feature zz, i.e., we evaluate the influence function of the functional at qq.

Proposition 1 (FIDgrad).

Assume Σg≻0\Sigma_{g}\!\succ\!0 and Σr≻0\Sigma_{r}\!\succ\!0. For a feature zz, let qϵ=(−ϵ)​q+ϵ​δzq_{\epsilon}\!=\!(1\!-\!\epsilon)q\!+\!\epsilon\delta_{z} with δz\delta_{z} a point mass at zz, and let u=z−μgu\!=\!z\!-\!\mu_{g}. Then ϵ↦FID⁡(qϵ,preal)\epsilon\!\mapsto\!\operatorname{FID}(q_{\epsilon},p_{\mathrm{real}}) is differentiable at ϵ=0\epsilon=0 and

rFIDgrad​(z):=−dd​ϵ​FID⁡(qϵ,preal)|ϵ=0=−2​(μg−μr)⊤​u−u⊤​(I−B)​u+tr⁡[(I−B)​Σg],r_{\mathrm{FIDgrad}}(z)\,:=\,-\tfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\epsilon}\operatorname{FID}(q_{\epsilon},p_{\mathrm{real}})\big|_{\epsilon=0}\,=\,-2(\mu_{g}\!-\!\mu_{r})^{\!\top}u-u^{\!\top}(I\!-\!B)u+\operatorname{tr}\!\left[(I\!-\!B)\Sigma_{g}\right], (7)

where B=Σr1/2(Σr1/2ΣgΣr1/2)−1/2Σr1/2B=\Sigma_{r}^{1/2}\!\big(\Sigma_{r}^{1/2}\Sigma_{g}\Sigma_{r}^{1/2}\big)^{-1/2}\Sigma_{r}^{1/2} is symmetric positive definite, and B=IB=I if and only if Σg=Σr\Sigma_{g}=\Sigma_{r}.

A positive reward identifies samples whose inclusion would decrease FID to first order. The first term captures the contribution of a sample to correcting the mean of the generated features, the second term captures its contribution to correcting the feature covariance. Figure 4 illustrates the resulting effect.

FIDgrad depends on both the current generated distribution and the individual image, so the same image can receive different rewards as the policy evolves. During training, we track the generated mean and covariance using exponential moving first and second moments. Each batch is scored before these estimates are updated, while the real-data moments remain fixed. Initialization and numerical conventions are specified in Appendix A.1.2. The resulting scores serve as terminal rewards in the group-relative objective.

4 Experiments

We train and evaluate Ponder policies for three generative models: MAR-B (Li et al., 2024, ImageNet,), MAR (Wewer et al., 2025, Sudoku; similar to SRM,), and the continuous-token text-to-image model MaskGen-KL-XL (Kim et al., 2025). All generators are frozen throughout our experiments. To speed up policy training, we use DDIM sampling with 25 steps for MaskGen-KL-XL and MAR-B, and flow matching (Lipman et al., 2023) with 12 steps for the Sudoku network. Policy training details are described in Appendix A.1, and generator architectures and inference settings in Appendix A.2. To our knowledge, PONDER is the first method to learn generation and revision order for continuous-token generators, so no prior method applies directly. We therefore construct baselines that isolate each component.

Visual Sudoku.

Following SRM (Wewer et al., 2025), we generate images of handwritten (MNIST) Sudokus. Such samples can look realistic while violating the Sudoku rules, making the task a test of global constraint satisfaction rather than local image quality. We classify every cell and verify the row, column, and box constraints, using SRM’s classifier and its easy, medium, and hard splits, which differ in the number of given cells. The frozen generator is an MAR (Li et al., 2024) with a flow-matching head operating on per-cell VAE latents (Appendix A.2, Table 7). A single policy is trained for all difficulty levels with a binary reward for a valid solution (Appendix A.1.4).

Learned ordering alone raises hard-split accuracy from 3.9% to 56.6%, well above SRM’s uncertainty-based greedy ordering (38.7%, Table 1); with a rethinking budget of R=9R=9, it reaches 96.7%. The resampling of patches itself only helps marginally: with random ordering, R=9R=9 leaves accuracy at 4.0%, and with the learned order but randomly chosen removal locations, it reaches only 62.7% compared to 56.6% with no rethinking and 96.7% with learned order and learned rethinking positions. The 34-percent gap to learned rethinking is therefore attributable to learning which predictions to revisit. The policy trained with R=9R=9 also generalizes to larger test-time budgets, reaching 98.6% at R=128R=128 (Figure 5).

ImageNet (MAR).

We apply Ponder to class-conditional ImageNet generation with the frozen MAR-B generator, training the policy with FIDgrad (Sec. 3.5). Since FIDgrad is computed in Inception feature space, we additionally report FDr-5 to check against reward hacking. It follows the FDr-6 metric of Yang et al. (2026) but excludes the Inception backbone, and thus measures Fréchet distance in five representation spaces that are not used by the reward (Appendix A.4). Without rethinking, Ponder reduces FID from 4.09 to 2.78 and increases IS from 181.22 to 206.55 compared with random ordering. FDr-5 improves as well (13.69 →\to 13.28). Increasing the test-time rethinking budget of the same policy to R=32R=32 further improves all three metrics, reaching 2.70 FID, 12.47 FDr-5, and 212.60 IS (Figure 6). Additional budgets are reported in Appendix Table 9. Figure 6 plots the corresponding FDr-5 trend.

Text-to-image generation.

We train two separate ordering policies for the frozen MaskGen-KL-XL generator. One uses Human-Preference-Score v2.1 (Wu et al., 2023a) (HPSv2) as reward on HPSv2 training prompts. We train it with a uniformly sampled rethinking budget from R=0R=0 to R=8R=8; each update uses one sampled budget for all trajectories. We evaluate on the official HPSv2 benchmark prompts and additionally report PickScore (Kirstain et al., 2023) and ImageReward (Xu et al., 2023). At R=0R=0, Ponder scores 26.50 HPSv2 versus 24.50 for random ordering in a separate evaluation. Increasing RR to 4 with the same policy raises HPSv2 to 26.95 and ImageReward from 0.68 to 0.73. At R=32R=32, HPSv2 reaches 27.80 and ImageReward reaches 0.81 (Figure 8). We train a separate policy with the same R∈{0,…,8}R\in\{0,\ldots,8\} mixture on the GenEval-style training prompts released by Flow-GRPO (Liu et al., 2025), using its dense partial-credit reward. We report the original binary GenEval metric (Ghosh et al., 2023). Results are shown in Tables 3 and 4. On GenEval, overall accuracy rises from 37.3% with random ordering to 41.1% with learned ordering at R=0R=0. At R=4R=4, the learned policy scores 42.6% versus 38.0% for random ordering (Table 4). Figure 9 shows the learned-policy test-time scaling trend.

5 Conclusion and Discussion

We present Ponder, a general framework for learning the generation order of frozen masked generative models. Rather than relying on fixed, random, or locally greedy schedules, Ponder learns a position-selection policy from rewards defined on the completed sample. The same policy can also revisit earlier predictions through rethinking, allowing decisions made with limited context to be removed and reconsidered once additional information becomes available. Across visual constraint solving, class-conditional image generation, and text-to-image synthesis, this improves the observed metrics over the generator’s default sampling schedule, while leaving the underlying generator untouched. Importantly, improvements are not limited to the reward we used. This suggests that the observed gains are not solely due to overoptimization of the training reward. Generation order thus becomes an optimizable component of the generative process rather than a predefined heuristic.

Limitations.

The policy adds a forward pass per generation iteration, which is small relative to the generative backbone and the scheduled denoising steps but adds a minor overhead. Its behavior is strongly dependent on the reward that is used for training. Reward design therefore remains a critical requirement for policy success. Finally, rethinking is governed by a prescribed budget and not allocated on demand. Learning when to stop, in addition to where to generate and revise, and extending the action space to inference parameters such as guidance strength, are natural next steps toward generative models that learn their own inference strategy.

Appendix A Appendix

A.1 Policy training details

A.1.1 Shared setup

The generators remain frozen while we train their ordering policies.

Trajectories within a conditioning group share generation noise, indexed by position and the number of previous fills. The policy observes the noise for each position’s next fill, while policy actions are sampled using a separate random stream. Evaluations use matched noise across rethinking budgets, with the noise capacity held fixed.

All ordering policies are bidirectional pre-norm Transformer encoders with GELU activations, learned positional embeddings, and zero dropout. Unless otherwise noted, each position’s input concatenates the frozen generator feature with the Gaussian noise for the next fill. Table 6 reports the trainable policy parameters and optimization settings.

All policies use Adam with ϵ=10−8\epsilon=10^{-8} and zero weight decay. During policy training, both the policy and frozen generator use bfloat16 mixed precision. Each update contains 128 independent conditioning inputs, each expanded into one group of trajectories. Evaluation precision is reported with each experiment.

A.1.2 MAR-B

We train the MAR-B policy with the FIDgrad reward and a rethinking budget of R=8R=8. The learning rate is held constant for 2,000 updates and then decays linearly to 2×10−62\times 10^{-6} over 2,000 updates.

At update uu, let (μu,Σu)(\mu_{u},\Sigma_{u}) denote the generated feature moments and (μr,Σr)(\mu_{r},\Sigma_{r}) the fixed real moments. For d=z−μud=z-\mu_{u}, the perturbation qη=(1−η)​q+η​δzq_{\eta}=(1-\eta)q+\eta\delta_{z} changes the mean and covariance to first order by dd and d​d⊤−Σudd^{\top}-\Sigma_{u}, respectively. Combining these with the derivatives of FID gives the reward in Eq. 7 under the assumptions of Proposition 1.

Estimated moments.

We maintain the generated mean μu\mu_{u} and raw second moment MuM_{u}, with Σu=sym⁡(Mu−μu​μu⊤)\Sigma_{u}=\operatorname{sym}(M_{u}-\mu_{u}\mu_{u}^{\top}). Every trajectory is scored using the current moments before they are updated. One trajectory is selected uniformly from each group of eight to estimate the batch moments. For selected features z1,…,znz_{1},\ldots,z_{n}, the updates are

μ^u\displaystyle\hat{\mu}_{u} =n−1​∑i=1nzi,\displaystyle=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}, M^u\displaystyle\hat{M}_{u} =n−1​∑i=1nzi​zi⊤,\displaystyle=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}z_{i}^{\top}, (8)
μu+1\displaystyle\mu_{u+1} =(1−α)​μu+α​μ^u,\displaystyle=(1-\alpha)\mu_{u}+\alpha\hat{\mu}_{u}, Mu+1\displaystyle M_{u+1} =(1−α)​Mu+α​M^u,\displaystyle=(1-\alpha)M_{u}+\alpha\hat{M}_{u}, (9)

with α=0.001\alpha=0.001. The moments are initialized from 50,048 separately generated images. Rewards use 2048-dimensional Inception features from the FD-Loss implementation (Yang et al., 2026) and fixed ImageNet-256 real reference statistics. Moment and matrix computations use double precision. Inverse square roots are computed by eigendecomposition, using a pseudoinverse on numerically singular directions.

Interpretation of the update.

The moving moment estimates and within-group reward normalization yield a surrogate objective for policy training. The resulting updates need not decrease population FID at every step.

A.1.3 MaskGen-KL-XL

We train separate policies against HPSv2.1 and the dense GenEval reward, using the same architecture and optimization settings in Table 6. The 553 official GenEval prompts (four images per prompt) are disjoint from the Flow-GRPO training prompts. We report the original binary GenEval score on these prompts.

A.1.4 MAR-Sudoku

We train the MAR-Sudoku policy with a rethinking budget of R=9R=9 and a terminal reward of 1 for a correct completed Sudoku and 0 otherwise. Training starts from partially filled grids. The number of given cells follows a triangular distribution with maximum density at zero and zero density at 81; their locations are sampled randomly.

A.2 Generator architectures and inference settings

Table 7 summarizes the generator architectures and inference settings. Generator parameter counts include the contextual backbone and shared generative head, but exclude tokenizers/VAEs, the MaskGen text encoder, and the Sudoku reward classifier. Both MaskGen-KL-XL policies use the architecture shown here.

For MAR-B, let CrC_{r} be the cumulative number of position decisions after round rr. The cosine schedule is

C0=0,Cr=max⁡{Cr−1+1,⌈272​[1−cos⁡(π​r128)]⌉},C_{0}=0,\qquad C_{r}=\max\!\left\{C_{r-1}+1,\left\lceil 272\left[1-\cos\!\left(\frac{\pi r}{128}\right)\right]\right\rceil\right\},

with the final cumulative count fixed at C64=272C_{64}=272.

MaskGen uses classifier-free guidance scale s=1+2​[32−max⁡(1,M)]/32s=1+2[32-\max(1,M)]/32, where MM is the number of masked tokens.

For MAR-Sudoku with gg clues, let W=81−gW=81-g denote the number of writable cells. A rethinking budget of RR requires D=W+2​RD=W+2R position decisions: W+RW+R fills and RR removals. If round tt makes KtK_{t} decisions and the trajectory has LL rounds, then

∑t=1LKt=D.\sum_{t=1}^{L}K_{t}=D.

All KtK_{t} decisions in one round share the same generator features, giving LL backbone evaluations. For Sudoku, Kt∈{1,2}K_{t}\in\{1,2\}. When W≥2​R+1W\geq 2R+1, using Kt=2K_{t}=2 for 2​R2R rounds and Kt=1K_{t}=1 for the remaining W−2​RW-2R rounds gives L=WL=W. Thus, on an empty grid with the training budget R=9R=9, the policy makes 99 position decisions over 81 backbone evaluations.

MAR-B and MaskGen-KL-XL use released pretrained weights without fine-tuning. MAR-Sudoku is trained for 500,000 updates with AdamW, (β1,β2)=(0.9,0.95)(\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.95), ϵ=10−8\epsilon=10^{-8}, weight decay 0.20.2, and a cosine learning-rate schedule from ×10−48\!\times\!10^{-4} to ×10−41\!\times\!10^{-4}.

A.3 Sudoku test-time scaling

Table 8 reports accuracy across rethinking budgets.

At R=9R=9, accuracy is 98.21%, 98.02%, and 97.94% across three evaluation seeds of the same policy, compared with 80.17%, 79.96%, and 80.29% at R=0R=0. For the first seed, the improvement is 18.04 percentage points.

A.4 MAR-B test-time scaling

Table 9 reports additional Ponder budgets together with random-policy baselines.

FDr-5 evaluation.

FDr-5 is the mean of the normalized Fréchet distances in ConvNeXt, DINOv2, MAE, SigLIP, and CLIP representations, excluding the Inception reward space, using the FD-Loss evaluator (Yang et al., 2026).

A.5 MaskGen preference test-time scaling

At test time, the policy uses one position decision per round, giving 32+2​R32+2R rounds for R∈{0,1,2,4,8,16,32}R\in\{0,1,2,4,8,16,32\}.

Training uses the official HPSv2 training prompts for the reward; evaluation uses all 3,200 HPSv2 benchmark prompts. All learned-policy budgets use the same start noise. We report HPSv2, PickScore, and ImageReward.
